Deep inside your brain hides a sheet of neurons almost nobody understood, until now.
It's called the claustrum, a thin sheet of neurons buried deep beneath your cortex.
Yale surgeon Yemi Damisah calls it the most connected region of the entire brain.
Nobel laureate Francis Crick suspected it was tied to conscious experience.
But it's so tiny and deep that electrodes almost always missed it.
On October 6th, Yale surgeons reported the first single-neuron recordings from the human claustrum, in seven epilepsy patients.
They used microwires just forty micrometres wide, while patients played a spaceship game dodging asteroids.
The neurons tracked uncertainty and prediction error, the signals of a brain learning what to expect.
So this hidden layer isn't just filtering the senses. It also helps drive behaviour.
